Notes: Year Established basis: Grey (2014, citing Aviam 2013) says Capernaum 'appears' to have been settled as a small Jewish fishing village on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee 'sometime in the second century BC', likely during the Hasmonean colonization of the region; 2nd c. BCE midpoint used (c.). Founding of the Jewish village. Grey n.15 adds the site was inhabited in the Bronze Age, abandoned in the Iron Age and 'possibly reoccupied on a limited scale during the Persian period' (not identified as Judean, so not used for Year Established).

Marc Turnage (CBN Israel): archaeological excavations indicate 'a population shift and growth took place in the first century B.C., in which the population became markedly Jewish'; he dates the village Jesus knew from c. 330 BCE (no ethnic identification for that phase). 1st c. BCE midpoint used (c.). Event: growth and Judaization of the village.

Loffreda (in Stern ed. NEAEHL 1993, quoted on this page): beneath the central nave of the limestone synagogue 'only a floor of basalt stones from the beginning of the first century CE was uncovered', possibly belonging to an earlier synagogue; Hellenistic-Roman houses found beneath the synagogue podium. Tzaferis (same volume, quoted here): 'The first inhabitants of the settlement were Jews'. Date c. beginning of 1st c. CE. Suggests an organized Jewish village community, possibly with a synagogue.

Jewish Virtual Library (Archaeology in Israel): 'During the period of Jesus' activity in the Galilee (beginning of the 1st century CE), it was a large Jewish village'; inhabitants were fishermen, farmers and merchants; Second Temple-period houses of basalt arranged in insulae around courtyards. Year c. 28 (Jesus' Galilean ministry, early 1st c. CE). No count given.

New Testament, Mark 1:21, 1:29: Jesus 'entered the synagogue and taught' at Capernaum on the Sabbath and then entered 'the house of Simon and Andrew' - a synagogue and named Jewish resident families (Simon Peter and Andrew). Date c. 28-30 CE (Jesus' ministry; c.). Organized Jewish community with a synagogue.

New Testament, Luke 7:1-5: a centurion in Capernaum sent 'some Jewish elders' to Jesus, who said 'he loves our people, and it is he who built our synagogue for us'. Attests Jewish elders (community leadership) and a synagogue in the village c. 28-30 CE (c.); the centurion himself was a gentile (Herod Antipas' service).

New Testament, Matthew 17:24: 'When they reached Capernaum, the collectors of the temple tax came to Peter' - collection of the Jerusalem Temple half-shekel tax at Capernaum, implying a Jewish community paying the Temple tax. Date c. 28-30 CE (c.). John 6:59 also places Jesus 'teaching in a synagogue at Capernaum'.

Jonathan L. Reed (Archaeology and the Galilean Jesus, 2000, pp. 151-152, as quoted by Heinrich 2013): estimate from the excavated single-story courtyard houses and the extent of first-century remains, population at the time of Jesus 'between 600 and 1,500 inhabitants'; midpoint 1050 used, range 600-1500. Total population of a village the source describes as laid out like Jewish settlements rather than Roman (no grid, unpaved streets). Year c. 30 (time of Jesus). Secondary citation of Reed; original not checked.

Matthew J. Grey (2014): first-century Capernaum 'had a population of between 1,000 and 1,500'; elsewhere 'the estimated 1,000 to 1,500 Jewish inhabitants of Capernaum' (explicitly Jewish). Basis (n.34): Early Roman remains extend only c. 300-500 m along the shore; excavators (Loffreda and Tzaferis; also Reed) estimated the inhabited area of 10-12 acres could hold 'no more than 1,500 inhabitants'. Midpoint 1250 used, range 1000-1500. 1st c. CE midpoint (50) used. Compare Gamla estimated 3,000-4,000 (same source).

Grey (2014): material culture shows inhabitants were 'mostly conservative (non-Hellenized) Jews': 'each of the excavated houses contained stone vessels (mostly cups) used for ritual purity washings'; 'no pig or nonkosher fish bones were found'; no miqvaot found ('the lake likely provided the means for ritual bathing'); Reed examined c. 150 stone-vessel fragments; residential structures 'built between the first century BC and first century AD' lie under the later synagogue. 1st c. CE midpoint used. Domestic evidence of a Jewish village population.

Cirafesi (Nordisk judaistik vol. 32 no. 1) on the scholarly consensus: Capernaum was 'a predominately Jewish village in the first century' (citing Chancey 2002: 101-5; Mattila 2015: 217-57); notes Epiphanius (Panarion 30.11.10) on later Jewish population. 1st c. CE midpoint used. No count.

Josephus, Life 72 (§403), Whiston transl.: during the revolt, after a skirmish near Julias/Bethsaida, Josephus's horse 'fell into a quagmire' and he was 'carried into a village named Cepharnome, or Capernaum' (reading of the name debated). Date c. 66-67 CE (Grey 2014 n.18 dates it ca. AD 66-67; c.). The village was then within the Jewish rebel-held Galilee under Josephus; no destruction of Capernaum reported. Population blank.
